title: Using APIs
text:
Taginfo
From OSM Wiki:

Taginfo is a system for finding and aggregating information about OSM tags and making it browsable and searchable. It was created by Jochen Topf.
You can try it out at: taginfo.openstreetmap.org. This is the main taginfo site and covers the whole

Why is this useful?
OpenStreetMap uses a system of 1 (combinations of keys and values) to describe geographic objects. Anyone can create new tags and add them to existing or new objects, making the map very flexible but also potentially confusing.
1 Refer to https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Tags for more information about what tags are and how they work.How can this help?
Taginfo provides data to adress questions such as:

How popular is a tag? How has this changed over time?
Where is it used?
What does it mean? How to use it?

Points, areas…
Is it used along other keys
Which are the possible values allowed?



GUI
Accessing taginfo.openstreetmap.org.






Figure 1: A screenshot from taginfo, displaying information about a given key (building)









CautionTask




Pick a key (or a tag) of your interest
Use the GUI to explore what it says about the them.
Can you answer any of the aforementioned questions about the tag?





API
Taginfo offers several endpoints. Each endpoint (and the parameters is accepting and the outputs) is documented here: https://taginfo.openstreetmap.org/taginfo/apidoc. As seen in Figure 2, there are multiple endpoints. Each of them is thoroughly described.






Figure 2: Screenshot of Taginfo’s API documentation









ImportantHow to read this?



Taginfo’s API documentation may seem daunting, but it provides key information that is important to understand:

path: is the url of the endpoint that we need to query
description: provides an explanation of what the endpoint does
format: explains the format in which the results are returned. In this case is a json file, which does not store information in rows and columns, and will need to be converted to a data frame.
paging: in this case is set to no, which means that all the results will be displayed in a single page/file.
sort: there’s no sorting
result: this lists every field contanined in the resulting json file, along with an explanation of their type and a description.
example: this provides a URL with a query. This is useful in two ways: 1) we can see the URL patterns, 2) we can see how a result would look like.
UI example: the equivalent query, as seen through the GUI (Website).




Quering Taginfo API with R
We will be using two packages: 1. {jsonlite}: to work with data stored in a json file. 2. {dplyr}: to manipulate a dataframe.

library(dplyr)
library(jsonlite)

selected_key <- "wheelchair"

# Set up the API endpoints URL
endpoint_chronology <- paste0(
    "https://taginfo.openstreetmap.org/api/4/key/chronology?key=", 
    selected_key
)

# Send a GET request to the API endpoint
response <- fromJSON(endpoint_chronology, simplifyDataFrame = TRUE)

# Save the data in the response (json) into a dataframe
key_chronology <- as.data.frame(response$data)

# We want to store the name of the key
key_chronology <- key_chronology |> 
  mutate(
    key = selected_key,
    date = as.Date(date)
  ) |> 
  relocate(key, .before = 1)


head(key_chronology)

         key       date nodes ways relations
1 wheelchair 2007-10-07     0    1         0
2 wheelchair 2007-10-26     0    1         0
3 wheelchair 2008-01-11     2    0         0
4 wheelchair 2008-01-12    12    0         0
5 wheelchair 2008-01-18     0    1         0
6 wheelchair 2008-02-04     2    0         0


We can even create some (basic) visualisations with that data:

# Plot cumulative way usage with base R:
plot(x = key_chronology$date,
     y = cumsum(key_chronology$ways),
     type = "l",
     lwd = 2, 
     col = "red", 
     main  = paste0("Cumulative '", selected_key, "' key usage on ways"),
     xlab  = "Date", ylab = "Ways (cumulative)"
)














CautionYour turn



Can you adapt the code to retrieve data from the prevalent values endpoint?

selected_key <- "wheelchair"

# Set up the API endpoints URL
endpoint_prevalent_values <- paste0(
    "https://taginfo.openstreetmap.org/api/4/key/prevalent_values?key=", 
    selected_key
)


# Retrieve key overview
response <- fromJSON(endpoint_prevalent_values, simplifyDataFrame = TRUE)
key_prevalent_values <- as.data.frame(response$data)

head(key_prevalent_values)

    value   count fraction
1     yes 2498034   0.6153
2      no 1026514   0.2529
3 limited  496817   0.1224
4    <NA>   38181   0.0094

title: Using APIs
text:
Overpass
Overpass is a read only API that retrieves map features containing a certain key or tag. It offers a way to query the map to look for specific features.
You can read more about it in the wiki: https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Overpass_API

GUI
Probably, the most popular way to intertact with overpass is through the web interface https://overpass-turbo.eu






Figure 3: Overpass-turbo screenshot displaying features containing artwork = * in Warwick’s campus



How to use it?
Overpass-turbo has a great documemntation in the “help” button, but a possible outline for basic usage could be:

Select the region you want to query the features, either by:

Navigating the map until the desired area
Typing the name of the location in the search box within the map

Use the wizard to build your query and providing keys (and optionally, values)







TipQueries



The Wizard builds Overpass queries from a short search expression. It understands the following conditions: Tag conditions

key=value — objects tagged key=value
key!=value — objects not tagged key=value
key=* — objects that have the tag key, with any value
key!=* — objects that do not have the tag key
key~value — objects whose key value matches a regular expression (append /i to ignore case)
~key~value — objects where both the key and the value match a regular expression
key!~value — objects whose key value does not match a regular expression
key:value — objects whose key value contains value
value — a plain search term is looked up among the known presets, e.g. “Drinking Water”




Run the query by either:

Clicking on “Build and run the query” (on the wizard)
Clicking on “Run” (main screen)

(optionallly) Export the results



API
Overpass API’s documentation is spread across multiple pages at OSM wiki: https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Overpass_API.

Quering Taginfo API with R
In this case, due to its relatively complexity, we will be using a specialised package to use Overpass API: {osmdata}.






TipHow to get a bounding box coordinates



Overpass needs a bounding box (usually shortened to bbox) is a rectangular area defined by two longitudes and two latitudes, where: - Latitude is a decimal number between -90.0 and 90.0. - Longitude is a decimal number between -180.0 and 180.0.
They usually follow the standard format of:

bbox = left,bottom,right,top
bbox = min Longitude , min Latitude , max Longitude , max Latitude

There are a number of websites to obtain the actual values for a given region, such as https://norbertrenner.de/osm/bbox.html



# Uncomment below if you don't have osmdata installed in your system:
# install.packages("osmdata")


library(osmdata)

Data (c) OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL 1.0. https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright
connected to: https://maps.mail.ru/osm/tools/overpass/api/interpreter

# Getting our bounding box

warwick_bbox <- getbb ("University of Warwick")
#warwick_bbox <- c(-1.57418,52.37887,-1.55783,52.38314) #Obtained from https://norbertrenner.de/osm/bbox.html

# See which server you're using
get_overpass_url()

[1] "https://maps.mail.ru/osm/tools/overpass/api/interpreter"

# Switch to a mirror
set_overpass_url("https://overpass-api.de/api/interpreter")

warwick_art <- opq(bbox = warwick_bbox) |> 
    add_osm_feature(key = "tourism", value = "artwork") |>
    osmdata_sf()

Waiting 14.9998378753662 seconds

# Explore the data
warwick_art

Object of class 'osmdata' with:
                 $bbox : 52.3706939,-1.5773781,52.3913551,-1.5490306
        $overpass_call : The call submitted to the overpass API
                 $meta : metadata including timestamp and version numbers
           $osm_points : 'sf' Simple Features Collection with 19 points
            $osm_lines : NULL
         $osm_polygons : 'sf' Simple Features Collection with 0 polygons
       $osm_multilines : NULL
    $osm_multipolygons : NULL




sf stands for Simple Features, and is a data type used to store geospatial information. Geospatial features can be: - points - lines - polygons (i.e., closed shapes) - multilines (a group of lines, not necessarily adjacent) - multipolygons (a group of polygons, not necessarily adjacent)
Refer to https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/ for more information.






ImportantUnderstanding osmdata objects



The warwick_art returned by our query is a list that contains multiple nested objects:

$bbox: the bounding box containing the features
$overpass_call: the call made to overpass api, using overpass syntax
$meta: medatada
$osm_points: a sf object containing points
$osm_lines: a sf object containing lines
$osm_polygons: a sf object containing polygons
$osm_multilines: a sf object containing multilines
$osm_multipolygons: a sf object containing multipolygons

For more information, refer to https://docs.ropensci.org/osmdata/articles/osmdata.html#the-osmdata-object




Creating a map
Let’s explore the actual data from overpass:

Indeed! Each of the column names are different keys from OpenStreetMap!




# Uncomment below if you don't have osmdata installed in your system:
# install.packages("leaflet")

library(leaflet)

# Save into a separate object to reduce typing.
points <- warwick_art$osm_points

# Create the interactive map

  addTiles() |>

We can do slightly better by adding some popups displaying the attributes:

# We create a new column aggregating multiple fields to be displayed in the popup

  mutate(
    popup = paste(

  addTiles() |> 
  addMarkers(
    data = points,
    label = ~name,
    popup = ~popup
  )

title: Using APIs
text:
Wrap up
In this session we’ve learnt a number of different things!

We got a theoretical understanding on strategies to work with big data.

And how API’s are examples of outscaling our infrastructure

Through interacting with two different API services we learnt:

We gained an understanding on how to get started with API services (e.g. documentation) and what to expect from them
We learnt how to interact via GUI and through code

When interacting with API through code, we learnt:

To use generic functions to query the APIs directly
To use specialised libraries to work with specific APIs


And we have also refreshed concepts from previous week: 1. Manipulating data using dplyr.

title: Week 9
text:
Computing averages by group
SELECT
  CASE
    WHEN wiki_url IS NULL OR wiki_url = '' THEN 'no wiki page'
    ELSE 'has wiki page'
  END AS has_wiki_url,
  AVG(CAST(count_all AS FLOAT)) AS mean_count_all
FROM keys_wiki
GROUP BY
  CASE
    WHEN wiki_url IS NULL OR wiki_url = '' THEN 'no wiki page'
    ELSE 'has wiki page'
  END;
or cluade
Notes:


Handling “missing”: Missing values can show up as NULL or as an empty string (''), and sometimes as whitespace. The IS NULL OR TRIM(wiki_url) = '' check covers all of these, so both are counted as “empty.”

GROUP BY wiki_status: SQLite and MySQL allow grouping by a column alias. PostgreSQL does too. In SQL Server or Oracle, you would need to repeat the full CASE expression in the GROUP BY clause or wrap it in a subquery.

Integer division: In some databases, AVG of an integer column may return an integer. If you see truncated results, cast it: AVG(CAST(count_all AS FLOAT)) (or AVG(count_all * 1.0)).

n_keys: I included a count of keys per group as a sanity check, which is useful context when comparing means. You can drop it if you don’t need it.


or an equivalent version in R, using dbplyr:
Reading on how to make connections via RStudio: https://rstudio-conf-2020.github.io/big-data/introduction-to-database-connections.html
library(dplyr)

keys_wiki_tbl <- tbl(con, "keys_wiki")

result <- keys_wiki_tbl |> 
  mutate(
    has_wiki_url = if_else(
      !is.na(wiki_url) & wiki_url != "", "has wiki page", 
      "no wiki page"
    ),
    count_all = as.numeric(count_all)
  ) |> 
  group_by(has_wiki_url) |> 
  summarise(mean_count_all = mean(count_all, na.rm = TRUE)) |> 
  # Collect results into a local dataframe (tibble).
  collect()

result
We can see these results:



has wiki page
937506.141317659


no wiki page
1682.56501885511



We can see there’s a huge difference between keys that have a wiki page and those that don’t

title: 1. Interrogating data locally
text: In this week, you will be using your laptops to work with a relatively big research dataset to answer actual research questions that arose from a research project.

title: 1. Interrogating data locally
text:
Session’s goals

Familiarise with the dataset (and the process it represents)
learn tidyverse’s syntax for frequent data manipulations:

filter() to subset rows matching some conditions
select(), to subset columns (by name or position)
group() and summarise() to compute summaries based on some criteria
join_by() to combine datasets

learn when to apply these methods to address research questions

title: 1. Interrogating data locally
text:
The data
The data consists of two csv files:

proposals.csv: containing all Approved, Rejected and Proposed tagging proposals from the OSM Wiki, as well as their associated metadata.
proposals_votes.csv: containing all the votes cast for every tagging proposal in proposals.

Both files were generated using a dedicated R-package called {OSMproposals} (Cámara-Menoyo 2026) which provides reproducible datasets containing information about OpenStreetMap’s tagging proposals. It does so by querying and webscrapping OSM’s wiki via helper functions. Refer to the official documentation page: https://warwickcim.github.io/osmproposals/ to see metadata and the source code that generated each dataset.

Cámara-Menoyo, Carlos. 2026. OSMpRoposals: Reproducible Datasets about OpenStreetMap’s Tagging Proposals. https://warwickcim.github.io/osmproposals/.






WarningImportant considerations




The provided datasets contain experimental versions of the actual datasets provided by the package, so documentation may slightly differ.
These datasets are part of an ongoing research. Please, do not share them beyond the classroom unless with explicit permission from their authors.









CautionIs this big data?





There are two ways in which data can be considered as big data:(Matter 2024):

Data that is difficult to handle: this could be either often because it has been “gathered from unorthodox sources, providing poorly structured data (e.g., raw text, web pages, images, etc.) as well as because of the infrastructure needed to store and load/process large amounts of data.”
Data that is hard to get value from due to size and complexity.





Matter, Ulrich. 2024. Big Data Analytics: A Guide to Data Science Practitioners Making the Transition to Big Data. First edition. Chapman & Hall/CRC Data Science Series. CRC Press, Taylor & Francis Group. https://umatter.github.io/BigData/.

Loading data
The data is provided by you in a folder data/raw/. It is a good practice to separate raw data (e.g. extracted from a package, survey…) from final data derived from code calculations. Final data can always be regenerated programmatically, whereas raw data can’t.








Load the two datasets and assign them, respectively, to the variables proposals and votes.






















CautionQuestions about the data




How was the data sampled?





Initial exploration
It is good practice to do some initial exploration to familiarise with our data. Some questions we may want to immediately answer are:

How big are these datasets?
What do they contain?
How complete each variable are? (i.e., missing data)

We can explore the first rows using head(), or, conversely, use tail() to see the last rows.














CautionQUESTION: Why would we need to use one or the other (or both)?














Use the tail() and pass the dataframe as first parameter and the number of rows in the second one.


tail(proposals, 5)
tail(proposals, 5)









Alternative, dplyr provides an interesting function gplimpse to describe the dataframes:








However, for large datasets like these, it would probably be better to see explore them interactively within RStudio or Positron’s GUI by running:
View(proposals)






WarningDid you notice something wrong with the data?





The column draft_started contains dates, but the column type is a character. This can be an issue if we want to make computations (like we are going to do in the next section), so we will need to fix this.
This is not the only problematic column. Can you find any other changes?





Fixing data
To fix the problem we detected, we need to change draft_started column type to a date, and we will be using mutate() to do so.















NoteHint 1





We are looking for a column name here. We need to write the name of the column that we want to convert to a date.











TipFully worked solution:





proposals <- mutate(proposals, draft_started = as.Date(draft_started))













Tip



Note that this syntax would be equivalent to base R’s syntax:
proposals$draft_started <- as.Date(proposals$draft_started)
At this moment tidyverse syntax may seem a little bit confusing and not very useful, but maybe the next bits can change our minds.










But actually, it’s more common to write this code using the pipe operator1 |>:
1 This operator allows for chaining multiple operations together, streamlining code.
The pipe operator (|>) takes the value of its left-hand side to the first argument of the function on its right-hand side. This enables a natural and readable way of chaining multiple functions together, reducing the need for intermediate variables and improving code clarity.

# Nested, reads inside-out
round(mean(log(c(10, 100, 1000))), 2)

[1] 4.61

# Piped, reads left to right
c(10, 100, 1000) |> log() |> mean() |> round(2)

[1] 4.61
















Important



Bear with me: we will see why this syntax using the pipe operator |> is very convenient.

title: 1. Interrogating data locally
text:
Answering questions through data

How diverse are the proposals?
On week 5 (Uprichard 2026), we saw the importance of measurments and how deciding what and how to measure is anything but trivial. There are many ways to define diversity. In this case, we will use the language in which the proposals are written as a proxy for diversity.

Uprichard, Emma. 2026. Lecture Slides - Week 5: Measurements. https://moodle.warwick.ac.uk/mod/resource/view.php?id=3277146.
We are going to use dplyr’s count() to count the number of different languages used in the column language.











proposals_lang <- proposals |> 
  count(language) # write the name of the columns

proposals_lang
proposals_lang <- proposals |> 
  count(language) # write the name of the columns

proposals_lang






count() conveniently can sort the values by number of uses:














CautionQuestion:



What does that information tell us? How is it related to diversity?




How much labour is required to make a proposal?
Again, there are multiple ways to define labour. One way could be to count time spent since their initial draft until the end of the voting process.






Important



Only a subset of proposals ever get to get voted, so we are going to use filter() to subset those proposals whose status is either Approved or Rejected and only select() the columns that are needed.


Here, we will be using select() to subset columns:











# Let's subset only the columns that are needed
time_spent_completed <- proposals |> 
  select(title, status_raw, draft_started, vote_end)

glimpse(time_spent_completed)

# Let's subset only the columns that are needed
time_spent_completed <- proposals |> 
  select(title, status_raw, draft_started, vote_end)

glimpse(time_spent_completed)


And now, let’s use filter() to subset rows whose status is either “Approved” or “Rejected”:










# Let's subset only the rows that are needed
time_spent_completed <- time_spent_completed |> 
  filter(status_raw %in% c("Approved", "Rejected"))

glimpse(time_spent_completed)
# Let's subset only the rows that are needed
time_spent_completed <- time_spent_completed |> 
  filter(status_raw %in% c("Approved", "Rejected"))

glimpse(time_spent_completed)










And now, we are going to compute the amount of time spent. We will be using mutate() to create a new variable called time_spent which is the time difference between the proposal was voted (finished) and drafted (started).










time_spent_completed <- time_spent_completed |> 
  mutate(time_spent = vote_end - draft_started)
  
time_spent_completed
time_spent_completed <- time_spent_completed |> 
  mutate(time_spent = vote_end - draft_started)
  
time_spent_completed








Tip



Remember when we spoke about the pipe operator |> ? We could pipe those two verbs in a single expression!










This new column time_spent says how much time each proposal took, in days2. We would need to have some nice summary statistics to have a good overview of the process.
2 Can you edit the code in the cell above to check time_spent data type? Is this what you would have expected?













Warning



We have some results that are either missing (NA) or negative values. This is because either the draft_started or vote_end values are missing. We should get rid of them to before proceeding.


But what if we wanted to see if there are differences between approved and rejected proposals? We will use group_by() to group by a variable and summarise(). to create new summary columns using some statistical functions:














CautionYour turn



Can you think of another variable we could use for measuring the labour involved? Could you do a similar process with this new variable?




How many votes did each proposal receive?
Votes are stored in a separate dataset proposals_votes, so let’s do some initial exploration














ImportantWide vs long data3



proposals_votes is a long dataset (as opposed to a wide one, like the previous one):

wide datasets: each row is an observation, refers to a unique value
long dataset: multiple rows refer to a same observation



3 For a more detailed explanation refer to https://tidyr.tidyverse.org/articles/tidy-data.htmlWe could use what we’ve learnt to count the votes for each proposal and type of vote being cast:








We can remove the proposals with no votes:









Reshaping dataframes
This format is not very useful for us now. It would be better to see how many votes of each type a proposal has received. In other words, we need to convert from a long format to a wide format. To do so, we will use another package from the tidyverse: {tidyr} provides two convenient functions pivot_wider()4 to convert from long to wide, and pivot_longer(), to do the opposite.
4 This function is full of nuances and requires having a clear picture of the actual data and what the shape we want it to have. Refer to the vignette vignette::pivot_wider or the help function ?pivot_wider









Combining dataframes
We have two datasets: one containing proposals, and another one containing votes. Wouldn’t it be nice to have the total votes per proposal in a single dataset?
To combine proposals with proposals_votes, we need to:

Make sure that both dataframes have a shared field to use as an index
Make sure that both dataframes are either long or wide

Gladly, both conditions are met, so we are ready to join them.










Piping everything
Or, we could do all of this (and something more) piping multiple verbs in one statement:














CautionQuestion



Can you guess what additional steps did we do and what are their outcomes?

title: 1. Interrogating data locally
text:
Further questions
By now, you should be equipped to answer the following questions by adapting the code above:

What gets proposed?
What’s the general outcome of the tagging proposal?
What are the more controversial proposals?

And questions related to measurement:

Has this process or its outcomes changed over time?
How can we operationalise diversity?

title: IM952 Labs
text:
The problem

Historically, Maps and power have gone hand in hand.(Crampton 2009; Harley 2008; Wood 1992)

Maps are never neutral: they have a political agenda (Haraway 1988; Harley 1989; Monmonier 2018)
Historically used for domination, control and/or surveillance (Foucault 1995; Scott 2020; Graham 2005; Edney 1999)




Critical and Feminist Geography have critiqued map’s objectivity:

Flagging (unconscious) bias by map-makers (usually men) (Monk and Hanson 1982)
Challenging positivist approaches and based exclusively in quantification (Pickles 1995)
Highlighting importance on what is being presented and silenced (Pavlovskaya 2009; Kwan 2002; d’Ignazio and Klein 2020)

title: IM952 Labs
text:
Object of study

OpenStreetMap: more than a map

OSM is the biggest and most precise free/libre spatial database of the world

It’s a Geospatial Database

9.1 billion nodes (2024-03-31) | Data under Open Database License (ODbL)
Flexible data structure based on key = value pairs

It is also a map (or a series of maps)

that have an opinionated representation of the database

It is a global and huge community (of 10,000,000 users worldwide!):

Anyone can contribute to it:
Adding / Editing map
Deciding what is included and how is represented

title: IM952 Labs
text:

title: Data
text:
The data
The data consists of two `csv` files:

proposals.csv: containing all Approved, Rejected and Proposed tagging proposals from the OSM Wiki, as well as their associated metadata.
proposals_votes.csv: containing all the votes cast for every tagging proposal in proposals.

Both files were generated using a dedicated R-package called {OSMproposals} (Cámara-Menoyo 2026) which provides reproducible datasets containing information about OpenStreetMap’s tagging proposals. It does so by querying and webscrapping OSM’s wiki via helper functions. Refer to the official documentation page: https://warwickcim.github.io/osmproposals/ to see metadata and the source code that generated each dataset.






WarningImportant considerations




The provided datasets contain experimental versions of the actual datasets provided by the package, so documentation may slightly differ.
These datasets are part of an ongoing research. Please, do not share them beyond the classroom unless with explicit permission from their authors.




Loading data
The data is provided by you in the data/ folder. We’ll load the two datasets and assign them, respectively, to the variables proposals and proposals_votes:

# Load dependencies
library(dplyr)

path_proposals <- "data/raw/proposals.csv"
path_votes <- "data/raw/proposals_votes.csv"

proposals <- read.csv(path_proposals) 
proposals_votes <- read.csv(path_votes)



Exploring data
Some questions we may want to immediately answer to familiarise with the datasets are:

How big are these datasets?
What do they contain?

title: Taginfo API
text:
library(httr)
library(jsonlite)

query_api <- function(key) {
  # Set up the API endpoint URL
  url <- paste0("https://taginfo.openstreetmap.org/api/4/key/chronology", "?key=", key)
  
  # Send a GET request to the API endpoint
  response <- GET(url)
  
  # Check if the response was successful
  if (status_code(response) != 200) {
    stop(paste("Failed to retrieve data from API. Status code:", status_code(response)))
  }
  
  # Convert the JSON response to a data frame
  data <- fromJSON(content(response, as = "text"), simplifyDataFrame = FALSE)
  
  # Convert the data to a data frame
  df <- data.frame(
    id = data$tag,
    date = data$date,
    nodes = data$nodes,
    ways = data$ways,
    
  )
  
  # Return the data frame
  return(df)
}
